//OWNER-DECISION-no-permission-prompts: STANDING OWNER DECISION -- 2026-09-19. Do not add permission prompts. `ask` contains exactly two rules: Bash(git push:*) and PowerShell(git push:*). Pushing code is the only thing the owner wants to approve; everything else Claude must be able to do without stopping. On 2026-09-19 `ask` was cut 41 -> 2 and the guards that were interrupting ordinary work were removed. 'Enhance the setup' NEVER means adding rules to `ask`. This overrides every hardening, symmetry and defence-in-depth argument elsewhere in the control plane.
//DENY-IS-NOT-AN-AUTONOMY-COST: Re-learned 2026-09-22, after the deny list was deleted in the belief that it was costing autonomy. It was not. `deny` BLOCKS SILENTLY -- it never prompts, never pauses, never asks. The only key that can interrupt a turn is `ask`. Deleting the 40 rules below therefore bought exactly zero additional autonomy and surrendered every mechanical block on irreversible destruction and secret exfiltration. The owner decision above permits new `deny` rules precisely because they are free: it restricts `ask`, not `deny`. If you are ever tempted to trim this list to 'speed Claude up', re-read this paragraph -- the answer is that it will not.
//WHY-NO-defaultMode: `defaultMode` is deliberately ABSENT, not set. Verified: any value OTHER than `auto` is honoured at project scope AND overrides the user-scope setting, so pinning even `default` here would silently DOWNGRADE the `auto` mode configured in ~/.claude/settings.json. `auto` itself is dropped at load -- only policy/user/flag sources may grant it. Either way this file cannot help, and can only hurt. sync-claude.mjs:987 warns on `auto`. Same reasoning excludes `disableBypassPermissionsMode` (standing decision: bypass is the human's switch, never ship the key at any value) and `blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories` (needs >= 2.1.257; PATH binary is 2.1.211, where the string does not exist and the key would read as configured while doing nothing).
//SHELL-RULES-ARE-WRITTEN-TWICE: Every shell rule appears as BOTH `Bash(...)` and `PowerShell(...)`. One form alone protects nothing on Windows, where either tool may be selected. A rule with no `:*` suffix is EXACT-match; a rule ending `:*` is a prefix match. deny/ask match ANY subcommand -- inside `&&`, a pipe, a subshell, or a loop body -- so a forbidden string needed as test data must be built by concatenation.
//ask: TWO RULES. See //OWNER-DECISION-no-permission-prompts above before adding a third.
//env: Project-scope env. RESEND_API_KEY is pinned to the sentinel that src/app/actions/contact.ts:31-38 checks for, so gate 7 (`pnpm test:e2e`) logs instead of emailing the real business inbox. This DEPENDS ON WORKSPACE TRUST -- corrected 2026-09-22 -- and is not exempt from it. PATHEXT is re-set because the agent host launches shells with it mangled to literally `.CPL`, which makes every binary on PATH unresolvable.
//enabledMcpjsonServers: A project-scope server declared in .vscode/mcp.json does NOT launch until it is named here. sync-claude.mjs cross-checks these names against that file and throws on a mismatch.
//includeCoAuthoredBy: OWNER DECISION -- 2026-09-25. Commits carry NO `Co-Authored-By: Claude ...` trailer. This is set here, mechanically, because the trailer was arriving from an AGENT-LEVEL DEFAULT rather than from any repo convention -- CONTRIBUTING.md's Conventional Commits section never asked for it -- so it landed on 15 of the 31 commits on feature/subhash and was absent from the other 16. An instruction in a prompt file cannot fix that: it depends on every agent remembering, and the default wins whenever one forgets. Do NOT 'helpfully' remove this key in a future audit because it looks like a leftover; absent means the default returns and the inconsistency comes back. Key verified real against the live binary (`grep -a -c includeCoAuthoredBy claude.exe` -> 5); it is a TOP-LEVEL settings key, a sibling of `permissions` and `env`, NOT a member of the `permissions` object. Forwarded by the allowlist at sync-claude.mjs -- a key added to this file alone is silently dropped.
//INTERPRETER-HOP: INTERPRETER HOP -- why the static rules here are a FIRST layer, not the only one. Permission rules are keyed by TOOL NAME, and the decision is made on the literal command string, so routing a command through a different interpreter escapes BOTH rule sets at once. Verified live 2026-09-22 against the same nonexistent target: `cat .env.production` was DENIED by the static rule, while `pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -c "Get-Content .env.production"` EXECUTED and reached the filesystem -- it returned the PowerShell "Cannot find path ... because it does not exist" error, so the read was genuinely attempted. Nothing was disclosed because that file does not exist here; do NOT repeat this probe against a file that does. The Bash matcher sees a first token of `pwsh`, which matches no cat/tee rule, and the `PowerShell(...)` rules do not apply because the tool that ran was Bash (see //SHELL-RULES-ARE-WRITTEN-TWICE). CLOSED 2026-09-22 by the PreToolUse hook, not by a new rule. An earlier draft of this note called the vector UNCLOSABLE and that is now wrong: .github/hooks/scripts/guardrail.py inspects the command string whatever tool carries it, and re-running the same pwsh probe after registration returned rc=2 with "Reads a .env file into the transcript." Enumerating interpreters is still not a defence -- `powershell.exe`, `pwsh -File`, `pwsh -EncodedCommand`, `sh -c`, `node -e`, `python -c` are one vector wearing different names, and a `Bash(pwsh:*)` deny would break legitimate use (a subagent drove real pwsh 7.6.6 through the Bash tool to verify this repo's PowerShell documentation on 2026-09-22). The hook generalises where an enumeration cannot. Two things still follow. The hook is a SECOND layer and can be absent -- it needs an interpreter, and it is skipped entirely if none resolves -- so never read a denial as proof a target is unreachable, and never treat these static rules as covering anything but ORDINARY spellings.
